sources.fact: Straus et al., 'A phylogenetic hypothesis for the origin of hiccough', BioEssays 25:182-188 (2003): hiccough may be the expression of archaic motor patterns, particularly gill ventilation in bimodal breathers such as most frogs; in gill ventilation the glottis is closed to prevent flooding the lung; hiccough is a burst of inspiratory muscles with glottal closure; circuit probably in the brainstem; hiccoughs occur in the human fetus and appear before breathing movements; neither model has experimental proof

Scientific American, 'The Evolutionary Origins of Hiccups and Hernias': according to one well-supported hypothesis, the hiccup motor pattern turns up in tadpoles that use both lungs and gills; they shut the glottis while sharply inspiring
Mayo Clinic, Hiccups: a spasm in your diaphragm causes your vocal cords to suddenly close, producing a 'hic' sound; see a provider if hiccups last more than 48 hours
NHS, Hiccups: they should only last a few minutes; see a GP if hiccups last longer than 48 hours
Cleveland Clinic, Hiccups: your diaphragm pulls down suddenly, making you quickly suck in air; the glottis suddenly closes; call a provider if hiccups last longer than two days

math.note: NHS and Mayo Clinic: more than 48 hours; Cleveland Clinic: two days

post.instagram_caption:
Your hiccups might be a leftover from ancestors with gills 🐸

In a hiccup your diaphragm suddenly yanks air in and your vocal cords snap shut. Tadpoles do almost the same move to push water over their gills: they suck in hard and shut the glottis so water can't flood their lungs. Scientists proposed the link in 2003. It's a hypothesis, not proven, but babies even hiccup in the womb before they start practicing breathing.

Hiccups usually stop within minutes. See a doctor if they last more than 48 hours.

Sources: BioEssays (Straus et al. 2003), Scientific American, Mayo Clinic, NHS, Cleveland Clinic.
